utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is the case IT-95-14/2-T (sic), the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry, I jumped the gun. Just before the next witness, Zlotrg, is brought in, I thought it might be helpful if I explained something about his evidence and how it may be possible to save time. He's one of two witnesses who are going to deal with the next municipality in order, Vitez. The witness who we've sent back for want of time will probably be able to give a greater overview of events than this witness, but this witness can deal with quite a large period of time. He was a police officer, and at one stage between December of 1992 and April of 1993, he made, and others in his office, made contemporary notes of particular events, and those notes still exist. In October of 1994, he made a detailed report to a judge, in respect of a pending case, which incorporated those notes covering the period December, '92, to April, 1993, and also covered events that went before that, and set out his then recollection, assisted by further events of what happened after that, namely, what happened to him when he was arrested and detained. And in 1996, he made another report, not specifically for the purposes of the OTP but for himself and for police records, I believe, again dealing with period 1, events that went before, the period of the notes, and events that happened afterwards. The two reports have been served, as I understand it, on the Defence, and they have possession of them. I'm not sure that they have, at the moment, possession of the original notes from the police station. They don't, but they exist and they can be made available to them. It occurred to me, and I discussed this with my friends yesterday, that certainly by the time we reach December, '92, it will save time and be the most efficient way of presenting evidence if he can simply read from the contemporary notes that he made, which were reflected in the two reports to which I've referred, and it may be that the Tribunal will take the view that it will be more efficient thereafter to allow him to refer to the reports for the period of time that came afterwards. I thought if I mentioned it now, rather than try and explain all that in his presence, it would probably be helpful. The first part of his evidence we'll deal with in the usual way, in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The name of the witness again, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Zlotrg. It's Z-l-o-t-r-g; first name, Edib. (Trial Chamber deliberates)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, what we've been considering is this: If copies of the notes were available for the Trial Chamber, since we are not in any national jurisdiction, is there any reason why we should not have the notes in front of us, and rather than laboriously reading through the notes, simply have them as the statement, as it were, in chief; your highlighting any parts you wish to highlight, and the Defence cross-examining on any part that they wish to cross-examine on?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I entirely agree. I can see no reason for that not to happen. And the only question would be whether one would take it further, for example, in relation to the report made to the judge in the High Court in Bosnia-Herzegovina in October, 1994, which sets out matters antecedent to and immediately after the contemporaneous notes, but of course it's a solemn occasion, making a statement to a court, and relying on those as well. But it may be best if we deal with things stage by stage. The contemporaneous notes are a discreet item and they are available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The notes may be, after all, the best record, rather than some later record, a statement made then at a subsequent time. If we had the notes in front of us, presumably it would be enough to start with. If anyone wanted to refer to the report for any particular reason, it could then be produced. But at the outset, it need not be, I should have thought. Yes, Mr. Stein.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I just want to make clear, as I understand it, there are three layers of notes, the original contemporaneous notes which Your Honours have just ruled on and on which we have no problem; a second layer, a 1996 compilation of all those notes, and then ultimately another layer in which the witness uses the notes to testify. The first layer, we agreed with opposing counsel. The second and third, I think, was just covered by your ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, at the outset, then, we will have the contemporaneous notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Shall I make -- I can make those available straightaway, because I know my learned friends, although they've seen the fruit of those notes in the two reports made in '94 and '96, I don't think they've have the originals yet. They've been produced in other trials, I believe. If those can be made available now, they are to become Exhibit 332,1, and then before very long, we'll reach a point where they cut in, because the evidence, although it starts in '91, it won't take very long before we get to the end of 1992. Probably by mid-morning break, I would have thought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And just to make sure, Mr. Nice, that I have the reports in order, Mr. Stein referred to a report or a compilation in '96. In fact, as I understand it, there was a report in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: October. Was that the one to the judge?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It was, indeed, yes, in a pending case where he was advised to tell the truth and instructed in his legal duties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then there was the later one made in '96 -- Mr. Stein got the order wrong, but I quite understand that -- which he made, as I understand it, both for himself and for general police records.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And what we are being handed are his notes for December, '92, until April, '93?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Can we have the witness, please? Mr. Nice, would you deal with one thing which is on my mind? What is the significance of "Z" on these exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I believe the Registry is better able to answer that than we are. That's the letter given to Prosecution exhibits in this case. Why I have "Z" or "Z," and I'm not going to be in any way nationalistic about the pronunciation of the last letter of our alphabet, I don't know. Perhaps I better say "Z" to show --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: We have some speculation on that, but I don't think we should share it. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would like to sit down.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your full name, please.

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Edib Zlotrg.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Age?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Nova Bila.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: By the time of the late 1980s, what job were you doing, and where were you living?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Until the end of the '80s, I was at the public security station in Vitez, and I lived in Vitez, Marsala Tita Street, Number 14A.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, you were in those services; does that represent the police? Is that the police?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just to go back a touch, what was your last job before being in the police?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: I was a car mechanic at the car repair shop in Vitez or, rather, I was a test driver and the shop steward in that shop in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you moved to join the police, roughly what year or precisely what year was it?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: I think it was 1986.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you join the police as a policeman to do police and detective work, or did you join the police to do some other type of work?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: No, I was responsible for equipment at the public security station.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What sort of equipment?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Armaments, ammunition, all of the -- all the gear for an active policeman. So that uniforms, the restraint means, and armaments, and the equipment and the gear of the regular police, and stationery.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In 1991, there were the elections in which the HDZ had local success. Did that lead to any changes in the arrangements at the police station?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Namely?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Pero Skopljak was appointed our head, and Saban Mahmutovic was appointed the commander. We worked normally, as before, until one point in time when the chief, Pero Skopljak, began to invite every individual employee of the Croat and Serb origin, and immediately after that, they began to separate from us and to put markings on their police uniforms of the Croatian Defence Council, and every day they were getting further and further away from the Muslim people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When was it, approximately, that this invitation by Skopljak to Croat- and Serb-origin employees was made?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: About a month or two after they took over the office, after he took stock of the situation at the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And a word or so about Skopljak: What was his background?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: I know that he was a priest in Vitez, and I guess he married and was thus expelled from the ecclesiastical orders. I was surprised, I saw his diploma, and I was really surprised to see that he had graduated from theology. At least, that is what he showed us, the document with which he proved that he was a graduate of a higher school of learning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You say that there was a distance being created between Muslims and the others. Can we now deal with something by way of detail: You had access to weapons because of your job?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What started to happen, or what happened, in relation to weapons, after Skopljak had taken over?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Mr. Skopljak began to take the rifles away from me, and the combat gear, and that is so many sets of ammunition for every automatic rifle. Naturally, he always signed receipts when he took them over. That armament, by and large, ended in the hands of the members of the Croat people. On a couple of occasions, I warned him that he could not behave like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: His reaction to your warnings?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: After, he exerted himself to remove me from that post so he could bring in his own man.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What methods of exertion did he use to try and remove you from your post?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: He called me to interviews with him, he threatened me with notice, and I told him that I could be removed only by the Minister of the Interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina from the job, because he was the one that had signed my appointment, and until I received a document to that effect, I would be responsible for the stored weapons and ammunition. That happened on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Eventually, did you lose or surrender your job?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes, in late '92 I moved over to the criminal investigation department of that same station.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And was that because you were dismissed by higher authority or because you surrendered the post? How did it happen?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: No, I did not want it to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So were you dismissed, or moved, by higher authority?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we move on in time, can you help us with a couple of things that Skopljak was doing in the course of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Nice --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Judge Bennouna, your microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Sorry, the previous question, I did not quite understand the answer. You said whether he was dismissed or moved by higher authority, and the witness answered "Yes." So it is "Yes," what? I think we did not get a clear answer to that, because you said either/or, and yet we received only one "Yes." So I should appreciate it if this could be clarified, please.

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: I was transferred to the criminal investigation department at the insistence of Chief Skopljak, and he brought in to my place, he put in his driver, Ivica Cosic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry if I didn't make that clear before. His driver, Cosic, did he have any experience, so far as you were aware, of dealing with weapons or the other equipment that had been in your responsibility and charge?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes. He was a policeman in the public security station, and for a while before I came there, he did do that kind of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Going back probably a little in time, but to deal with the activities of Skopljak, was there an incident involving some FAP trucks that occurred?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you tell us quite briefly what happened?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: I do not recall the date, but I remember coming to work, and then we found two drivers in the room where officers on duty were. If I am correct, they came from Vogosca, and they were transporting two vehicles, two FAP vehicles, full of fuses for the plant in Vogosca. The transport had been announced, had been reported to the public security station properly, and this station was to supply the escort. However, they were intercepted somewhere between Vitez and Busovaca, at a place called Klupe, and according to the driver, they were taken to Mt. Kruscica, to the area of Zabrdje, municipality of Vitez, and they were left there during the night. However, my fellow policeman at the police station, Mirsad Tatarevic, found the trucks in Tisovac, a municipality of Busovaca, covered, camouflaged, with branches. According to his statement, Vlado Ramljak, a policeman, on one occasion at a hotel, told Mirsad that Mr. Pero Skopljak had ordered him to intercept the trucks and liquidate the drivers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were the drivers ever seen again?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes, that morning, they came to report. Had they been liquidated, they would not have come to report that they had been robbed. But it was Romljak who said that this was the first task of that kind, and that he simply could not perform it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So the fuses, what were the fuses for, what sort of equipment? If you know; don't guess if you don't.

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: I think for shells, because Vogosca, I think, made shells.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And so that landed up in Tisovac?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The second thing about Skopljak is his movements to and from Grude.

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Every week, Pero Skopljak took the official vehicle and the driver, Ivica Cosic, and went to Grude. And according to Cosic, whenever they would come back from Grude, it would be either escorting a truck with armaments or bringing in weapons to Vitez in the official car of the public security station for the Croat people. And Ivica Cosic was criticising me for not arming ourselves, because, allegedly, Croats were defending us as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did any of the weapons allegedly coming back via this route find their way into Muslim hands or not?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: No, not at least as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: These last two matters you've helped us with, the convoy -- the two lorries, rather, with the fuses, and the trips, Skopljak to Grude, did they happen in 1991, or 1992, or can't you remember?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: '91, because in 1992 I was not the head of the equipment depot.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You did tell us that you lost your job or changed jobs at the end of 1992?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But you say in 1992, you weren't in charge of the depot, so you had lost that earlier?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: It means on the 30th of December, that was when I turned over the stock, when the inventory took place. No, sorry, they went to Grude in '92, that is where I went wrong, because I spent the whole of '92 at the depot, so I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I want you to stick with 1991, just to deal with things, insofar as we can, in periods of time. What, if any, changes for the life of Muslims in Vitez happened in the course of 1991, in general?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: First of all, pressure was exerted against the Muslim population. Armed members of the HVO were patrolling Vitez, and they were using derogatory terms against the Muslims, against the president of the presidency. They were dismissed from work.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Any other events or types of events that you can now recall?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Well, since the conflict with the Serbs had already started in Bosnia, then the members of the Territorial Defence were called up for work duty. Otherwise, they would not be receiving the aid that they were entitled to receive. So quite a few members of the Territorial Defence went back to work and returned everything that they had received from the units to the units, themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As between groups of different ethnic origins, had there been friction in the late '80s or in 1990 in Vitez or not?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: No, there wasn't any friction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: By 1991 and the end of 1991, was there any display of friction or of tension between the groups of people of different ethnic origin?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: As far as I know, there weren't any conflicts of wider proportions. Perhaps there was a squabble or two, but there was nothing, really, in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did there come a time when ethnically-based songs, for example, were to be sung by one group or another?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Well, I already said that the members of the HVO and the members of the HOS sang songs glorifying the Ustasha movement and insulted everything that was Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's move to 1992. The changes that you've described in 1991, did they continue, or get less, or get worse in 1992?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: They got worse.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I want you to deal with some specific incidents. Try and date them, if you can. Was there an incident involving a man called Trako, T-r-a-k-o, in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes. Samir Trako, nicknamed Crni. I think in May, 1992, he was killed in the hotel in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How was he killed?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: He was hit by two or three bullets from an automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who was the officer on duty in the police station at the time?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: I don't know who the policeman on duty was, but I know that I was the criminology technician on duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And for a murder case or a killing of this kind, was it your duty to attend the scene?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Indeed, when you attended such a scene, did you go alone or did you go with another official?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: No, I would go with the entire team for the investigation. It consisted of an investigating judge, the prosecutor, the operative worker of the police station, that is to say, the public security station, and the criminology technician.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When did you get to that scene first?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: The next morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was that normal or was there any reason why there was a delay between one day and the next?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: It was not normal. I wasn't even notified of the event. It is only when I came to my regular work that I was informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: By whom?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: The man on duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Samir Trako, what ethnic group did he come from?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you got to the scene with the team, what did you discover?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: We found what we were shown by the members of the HVO. That is to say that we found the alleged scene where the crime was committed, where the murder was committed. As far as I remember, there were only two holes in the glass and a small blood stain. And I think there is a record that was compiled by the judge from the basic court in Travnik, because my notes, related to this case, remained in Stari Vitez and were destroyed. However, we asserted straightaway that that murder had not been committed there, because there would have had to be more traces. We should have seen more than we were presented by the members of the HVO. And then, on the other hand, we did not find the perpetrators of the crime at the crime scene. According to the commander of the military police, Ivan Budimir, he had run way, which was illogical. I mean to have a man escape from headquarters of the military police, full of military police, and that he tried to escape from there and that he was shooting. That is what they claimed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm just going to cut across you there with this question, for explanation purposes: You say that a man was -- "for a man to escape from the headquarters of the military police." Although this happened at the Hotel Vitez, what was the Hotel Vitez used for at the time?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: It was the headquarters where Mario Cerkez was. I don't know what his function was, whether he was commander of the brigade or commander of the staff. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were the premises staffed by military men or women?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes, members of the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And were they armed?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes, yes, they were always armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And what was the overall account for this killing that was given to you, at your investigation, by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: They said that Trako tried to enter the premises where the military police was and that the officer on duty, Vukadinovic, had warned him and then shot at him, although Trako was unarmed. And the commander of the military police, Ivan Budimir, put him into his car and took him to Travnik. Together with Trako were two other Muslims whom the military police of the Croatian Defence Council also took in an unknown direction, unknown to us. And only a day or two later, they were handed over to us, but they had been beaten up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, may I just have a clarification? The witness said that Trako tried to enter the premises where the military police was and that the officer on duty had warned him and then shot at him. And then comes the part that I'm interested in, "although Trako was unarmed." Was that something that was said to the witness, or does that reflect his own judgement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that he was not armed for the following reason: The Territorial Defence did not have any weapons, so all our weapons were at the front line. So a member of the Territorial Defence units would go to the front line, fight there for a while, leave his weapons there and then go back, and they would be replaced by others. And this is a statement that was made by Ivan Budimir and the rest. Also, we did not find any weapons while carrying out the post-mortem on Trako Samir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What did the HVO say, if anything, about whether the man had been armed?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: They didn't say anything in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just that he tried to get into the premises?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I hope that meets Judge Robinson's concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were telling us about how two other men had been with Trako and had been beaten up before being handed over to you?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Those two men, what were their names, if you can help us?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: One was Petak, and the other person's last name was Trako as well, but I really can't remember their first names. But there are medical documents concerning their condition when they were handed over to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just "Yes" or "No." Were they able to give you any account of what had happened at the killing?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: I did not talk to them. That was most probably done by the security officer at the command of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And that officer would be -- can you help us?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Efraim Pinjo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you, yourself, see those two other men when they were handed over?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So you formed the view that the scene that you were shown was not, as it were, a true scene?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: First of all, as far as the shooting wounds are concerned, and obviously he was shot most probably by an automatic rifle, probably a big calibre, 762, I can't remember exactly, but most probably so, and he was shot at from a very short distance, so there must have been more bleeding. Another thing. When a wounded person is carried from the place where he is wounded, through this kind of a hallway, which is about 10 metres long, I think, there had to be blood stains, blood stains on the floor in this hallway. However, we did not see any of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kovacic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. President, of course I'm trying to avoid any kind of objections because we work here in a different way, but the witness has not been identified as an expert and now he's giving us an expert opinion on the wounds. If the Prosecutor has grounds for this to explain how qualified the witness is in forensics, then perhaps we can have this line of questioning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just help us, please, Mr. Zlotrg: In the course of your work dealing with equipment and firearms, had you had to visit other scenes of killings, or not?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Not only that, I was a criminology technician, and I conducted such crime-scene investigations in cases of suicide and murders. And my job as this kind of a technician is to take pictures of every wound, to identify them, and after all, we were taught, in order to become criminology technicians, what an exit wound is and what kind of bleeding there is when there is an exit wound, an entrance wound, and that's my job. (Trial Chamber deliberates)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we find that he is sufficiently expert for these purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Returning to the question of blood stains in the hallway, you didn't see any of those where you expected them. Any other features of the scene that you haven't covered already that alerted your suspicions?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: There were two holes in the glass door, and 5 or 6 metres away from that is another glass wall which was not affected by bullets or anything else. I think that a bullet that would pass through one piece of glass would have to, if not break, then at least damage this other glass pane. But we never found anything like it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you ever find evidence of any other scene where the crime may have been committed, or not?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: No. No. We were not even allowed to go further.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The delay between the alleged time of the killing and your arrival, whose responsibility was that? Who had caused that delay?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, the policeman on duty, instead of informing the members of the investigation team -- that is to say, instead of informing me, the operations worker, that is to say the inspector, the investigating judge of the basic Court in Travnik, and the office of the prosecutor, he called the head of the police station, Pero Skopljak, and Pero Skopljak ordered me to have Mr. Vladimir Santic taken to the crime scene for investigation, and Mr. Franjo Sucic, who was a criminology technician. They did go to the scene of the crime, and what they did, I don't know. I just know that the next day, when we arrived at the scene of the crime, it was not properly secured by policemen, and I think that the investigating judge stated this in his report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I don't know if you're going to move on, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I am going to move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- as a matter of principle in this case, I wonder how much we are going to be assisted by very great detail about individual crimes, serious though, of course, they are, in other cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. It depends to whom this crime may be directly connected in due course, but I've dealt with what I want to deal with by way of the scene, and I've got a couple of more questions to ask, and then I think I probably will be moving on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was anybody ever arrested for this crime?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was anybody ever identified by the HVO at the scene as responsible for the crime?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes, Vukadinovic. I think his first name is Perica. He's a military policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And what happened so far as he is concerned?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: He went away in an unknown direction. He had weapons too, but then after a few months, he walked about Vitez as a free man.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, I want you to answer the next question simply "yes" or "no"; do you understand me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Nice, may I interrupt you for a moment. You asked a question, if anyone had been identified by the HVO as responsible for the crime, and the witness's answer was yes, and he gave you a name. How does the witness know? Is it direct knowledge, or hearsay, that he learned that the HVO has identified somebody as responsible for the crime? Because he answered in the affirmative, and I believe it would be good if it could be clarified during this session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: The report says so, that Perica Vukadinovic shot, and also the statement made to the investigating judge, that he was the one who did the shooting and then ran away from the scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you say which member of the HVO provided that detail?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Since Ivan Budimir was commander of the military police, and he was present during the investigation of the scene, I think that he was the one who made the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Coming back to the question that I had asked you, I want you, please, to answer the next question simply yes or no. Do you understand me?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were there rumours as to who had committed this crime? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And again, I don't want you at any stage at the moment to mention the name of the person against whom the rumours were made. I just want you to tell us, as it were, how close or far from any source --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, just a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The judge's microphones are on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, we don't want to hear about rumour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I've used the word "rumour" in order to characterise what may be second- or third-hand hearsay, rather than to use a technical term, and I was simply going to discover from the witness at what state of remove he had any information to help the Tribunal. I'm quite happy to leave it there because I suspect, although I can't be sure, that the answer would not be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Your characterisation of "rumour," of course, we understand as not trying to denigrate the evidence. But nonetheless, that is in effect what it would be, and as a matter of principle, as I say, we are against hearing evidence of rumour because it is liable to be completely unreliable. We could place no reliance on it when coming to any sort of verdict. So if you would bear that in mind, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. We may, on a future occasion -- I'm not going to take it further with this witness, but we may on a future occasion have to find another formulation of words, because "first- and second-hand hearsay" is very much a technical term of art with which we are comfortable and witnesses may not be, but in any event, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next event is one I want you to help us with, I think a little later, but give us the date, if you can. Was there an occasion when Muslim policemen in the police station were disarmed?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When, and just in a couple of sentences, the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: I do not remember the exact date. It says so in my statement, but I think it was sometime in June or July that Darko Kraljevic, the then-commander of HOS, barged into the police station with HOS units and disarmed Tatarevic Mirsad, Hrustic Safet, and a few other policemen, locked them up, came back after a while and said that they could be released because they didn't need hostages. That is the first time that we members of the Muslim people were expelled from the police station. We were not allowed access into the police station any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Any reason given for disarming these people?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Well, we didn't sign -- we didn't sign a paper saying that we would join the police force of the so-called Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And whose condition had that been?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: The Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who in particular, if anyone, had made it clear that that was a condition of your continuing employment?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: After that, they had a competition, and they took the Muslims whom the Croatian Defence Council and the SIS liked.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, and who did that include? Did that include you?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes. I was kicked out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But when you say it was a condition of signing, who expressed to you or to your colleagues that you had to sign up to the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna? Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly. I think all of it started from Pero Skopljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So you were now out of the police station?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes, and all members of the Muslim people who did not want to state their loyalty, not only us. I mean, even the employed in the municipal offices in the municipality of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How did you spend your time for the next weeks and months?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Contacting the Ministry of the Interior in Sarajevo, and they told us to keep quiet, that is, to stay at home and wait.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the event, did you continue to receive your salary or not?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: From the Ministry, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Vitez municipal Territorial Defence headquarters had a logistics section?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there an incident there that you can tell us about?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes, though it was a long time ago, and I don't remember the date, but I suppose you have the date. The Croatian Defence Council attacked, and I know that two policemen took part in this. Vladimir Jukic and Vlado Ramljak participated in the attack, and I know that on that occasion they captured Muharem Kurtovic, Cazim Ahmic, and Patkovic; I can't remember his first name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was the reason for this attack, so far as it could be judged?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Because they were members of the Territorial Defence. And looted, because after that, they plundered, they looted, and massed the stocks that belonged to the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What sort of stocks were they?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Food, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did Skopljak stay in his job as chief of police or did things change?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: I think in September, when the politicians agreed that the police should start working together again, then Pero Skopljak was removed and replaced by Mirko Samija, the judge of the basic court in Travnik. That is when we began to function together again, I mean, the police station, rather, the public security station.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So having been at home and keeping quiet for a couple of months or so, you now returned to the police station?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And for what period of time were you able to work effectively, or at all, in the police station?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: I don't quite understand. Since the return, or generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: After that return. When Skopljak was replaced and you returned.

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: About a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the dates that are in the statement are not in dispute, it would probably be helpful if my friends told me, and then I could simply put the dates to the witness rather than lack precision where precision may ultimately help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is there any objection to that course?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Frankly, with the six statements that we have, I'm not clear on the dates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So that it may be simpler if the witness clarified the dates?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Exactly. If he can, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. But it may be simplest to put them to him directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He's referred on several occasions to his statement. And for the assistance of Mr. Stein, the statement that I'm looking at is the one of the 27th and 28th of September, which is probably the most comprehensive. I'm on page 4 of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Which year?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 1997. And indeed, I'm going to put the dates of the last four events to the witness, starting at the top of page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In your statement, Mr. Zlotrg, you said that the occasion when Darko Kraljevic disarmed Muslim policemen was the 18th of June of 1992; that the attack on the logistics section was approximately the 24th or 25th of June of 1992; that Skopljak's replacement by Samija was on the 21st of September of 1992; and in line with what you've just said about working for about a month, that you worked together until about the 20th of October, 1992. Those are the dates you've put out in your statement. When you made your statement, were you able to either recall or research material to establish those dates?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Well, to begin with, I was born on the 21st of October, so that I associated it with that. That is why it was fixed in my memory. Secondly, as I have said, I had my journal, and I noted down all those events, and also in the archives of the police station you can find those events recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So the month of working together ended on the 20th of October, and what were the circumstances in which that cooperation came to an end?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: In the morning, I started for work, and naturally, as I came near the station, I noticed members of the Croatian Defence Council under full combat gear standing in front of the station. The flag, the Croatian flag, had been hoisted in front of the building. So I realised that something was wrong and I started towards the command of the Territorial Defence staff. On my way there, midway, I met the commander of the station of the public security station, Mr. Saban Mahmutovic. He asked me where I was going, and I described to him the scene in front of the public security station. I told him that it would be better for him too, to also come with me to the headquarters to see what it was all about, but he insisted on going back to the station to see with his own eyes what was happening there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you go back with him or did he go back alone?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: We went back together.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: When we entered the station, since our offices are on the first floor, we started up the stairs, but a policeman who had allegedly been on a sick leave because of some heart problem, Ivo Perkovic, was in full combat gear, and he ran up the stairs in our steps, following us, and ordered us to come down, that we could not come upstairs. But Saban Mahmutovic asked him, "Well, who is the commander here, me or you?" And he went on, and I returned to the room of the officer on duty. And there I saw about 10 members of the police in full combat gear, that is, with armaments, with rifles, and Mirko Samija, the chief or so, in the uniform. It is the first time I ever saw him in a camouflage uniform. And there I waited for my commander. And after about 50 minutes, he came back and said, "Mirko, what does all that mean?" And Mirko told him, "Well, don't you see?" And we left the public security station and returned to it only in November, '97.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You say that the Croatian flag was hoisted on the building. Are you able to be specific about which flag it was that was hoisted?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: The flag of the State of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Nothing to do with Bosnia-Herzegovina at all?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: None.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was a meeting arranged for later in October?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: By whom and for whom was the meeting arranged?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: It was organised by Mirko Samija, the chief, in order to again start the joint work of the police station in Vitez. He invited us to discuss how we would go on working together.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You attended the meeting; what were the terms?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes, all the employed were present at the meeting, that is, Croats, Serbs, and Muslims. And when we entered the hall in the municipal hall of the municipality of Vitez, Mr. Samija opened the meeting and told us straightaway to fill in application forms, the Ministry of the Interior of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna with the seat in Mostar, which meant to give notice of leave to the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And those who had filled those application forms still did not have his work guaranteed. But he said, "After you pass SIS tests,..." that is, the Security and Information Service tests, "... only those who pass the SIS test may get the job," so that no one was guaranteed work.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was your reaction to this proposal or this requirement?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Well, one of us asked him -- at first we refused it, naturally. And then we asked him, well, how did he intend to make public order in purely Muslim villages such as Preocica, Bukve, Kruscica and other places. And he said that his police would do that, armed with rifles, with helmets and bulletproof jackets. And then the rest of us left the meeting, because we realised that the meeting had been convened simply to bring the pressure to bear on us, to make us join the Ministry of the Interior of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And did all the Muslims leave the meeting or did any stay behind?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: We all left the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was a further meeting held that same day by you and your fellow Muslim policemen?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The decision that was made?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: That we should send a request to the Ministry of the Interior to form a police station in Stari Vitez, in Old Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Stari Vitez being part of Vitez or a separate community?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: It's a part of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If and when we look at a map of Vitez a little later, we can point it out then. The decision was made to set up then, the police station in Stari Vitez. How quickly was that decision put into effect?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: We were allowed, by the Ministry of the Interior, to form and to set up a police station in Stari Vitez only as late as November.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we come to that, there's something else that I can fit into a chronology of events, and the Defence will be assisted by knowing that it's the statement of the 4th of February of this year, a short statement that deals with it. Was there, in October of 1992, an agreement made between residents of Ahmici and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you aware of it at the time or not?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you come into possession of the material documentation?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you look, please, at Exhibit 245? You have before you a document --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could it be put on the ELMO, because the interpreters do not have it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm so sorry. A copy can be brought around to the interpreters straightaway. It's my mistake for not having provided this one in advance, and I apologise to the interpreters. The English version is on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you have a document in your own language with some signatures at its foot?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So far as the signatures are concerned, some being said to be for the HVO and some for the Muslim people, are you able to recognise any of them?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Which ones?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Muris Ahmic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It would help if you identify which side it's on, HVO or Muslim, and which number it is; first, second, third, if there are three.

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: For the Muslim people, the first signature. Fahrudin Ahmic is the third signature, and Islam Ahmic is the fourth signature. As for the second one, I'm not quite sure. I think it's Nazir or Nezir Ahmic. I'm not sure. I didn't know you would be asking me that because I do have them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were these men known to you at the time, or people known to you at the time?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are any or all of them still alive?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Not one of the four of them is alive. They were killed on the 16th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The agreement itself, if you follow it in the original, I'll read the English translation. It's an agreement between the HVO, Croatian Defence Council, Santici, and representatives of the Muslim people of Ahmici, concluded at the home of Nenad Santic on the 22nd of October, 1992. "4.00 p.m. The Muslim inhabitants of Ahmici are required to make a list of their weapons and submit them to the HVO in the interests of preserving the peace in Santici and Ahmici. To this end, the HVO Santici shall provide every guarantee to and ensure the safety of the Muslim people in these areas. The HVO will, in the foreseeable future, establish a mixed unit of Croats and Muslims for the purpose of defending the area from the aggressor Chetniks. "The mixed unit, that is to say the Muslims from this unit, will not be used in combat actions against the Muslims or the Croats in any area. "On the basis of the above, the return of both Muslim and Croatian refugees to their homes is guaranteed, as is their peaceful coexistence. This guarantee shall be provided by the mixed unit of both parties." Does what I have read out, translated by the interpreters, match what is on the document?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then picking up the history of events that more closely at the time concerned you, you say that the station was not set up, I think, until November or December?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Late November.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we come to that, was there an incident involving a man called Kargic and Hurem and a Yugo motor car that you can tell us about?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes. They were Territorial Defence members who were killed, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The date you've given in your statement --

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Just a moment. There was somebody -- there was somebody who sustained severe injuries, but I can't remember the name now. The name escapes me, but he was also a member of the Armija. Minet Akeljic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Would you like me to put the date to you from your statement?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Will you read it, please? There are so many of those dates that --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The 19th of November. By the time of this incident, had the station in Stari Vitez been established or not?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: I don't think so, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In any event, learning of the death of these two men and the injury of the third, did you take any action in your official capacity, or in your capacity as a policeman, or did you attempt to take such action?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes. I was providing technical assistance to the police during the inspection on site, because they did not have a technician, a criminal technician. So that's when I was notified of the event. I first went to the command of the Territorial Defence headquarters, and when they informed me about all the details that were accessible to them, I went to the military police of the Croatian Defence Council and talked there to Marijan Jukic. I don't know if he was the unit commander or whether he was a member of the military police. And he told me that for reasons of security, we should try to defer the inspection until the next day, because there was dense fog and the tension was very high. And after that, I went to the civilian police of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to just pause for a minute. You and your fellow Muslim police officers had ceased working at and from the police station where the HVO were. You had yet or may have had yet to establish your own police station. But in this intervening period of time, were you performing police work at all or not?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So the initiative you took on this occasion, was it, as it were, as a citizen or as a policeman about to be established at Stari Vitez? What was your capacity?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: I was there as -- well, how shall I put it -- an extramural associate of the military police of the Territorial Defence headquarters, because they did not have that kind of personnel and I was reluctant to leave the police, the police work, so that this technical professional part of help during the on-site investigation, which was to be done by the army by statute, because if the crime involves military, then it cannot be the civilian police which will do such an investigation. And then the TO commander took me on to perform all those duties as a criminal technician for the military police, and that it was in that capacity as a technician familiar with the criminal investigation that I worked for.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you for explaining, and you just previously had told us that you were going to conduct the on-site investigation on the following day. On that day, where did you go first?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: The team which arrived from Zenica, that is, the higher military prosecutor, military judge and the team of the security service from Zenica, and so we were dealing with the murder. At 9.00 they arrived to the station in Vitez, that is, the station of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What happened there?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: And then the inspector from Zenica requested that we go to the Territorial Defence headquarters to get the particulars about the dead and to conduct an interview with their superiors.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you go off to do that and, on the way, reach the Vitez petrol station?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: We did go to the headquarters, and we finished there. The headquarters gave us a vehicle and a driver. And the criminal investigation also attached to us a man from their office, Ramo Vatres, to attend the on-site investigation. And as we went there to the scene of the crime next to the petrol station in Vitez, members of the military police of the Croatian Defence Council appeared in front of us, aimed their rifles at us, and stopped the car and made us, at gunpoint, get off that vehicle. I tried to explain to a policeman that we were a team, that we were a part of the investigation team, and they could not begin with the investigation until we arrived, and that it had all been agreed with the commander of the military police, or whoever he was, Marijan Jukic. And he simply pointed his rifle at me and made me move towards the hotel where the headquarters of General Blaskic were at the time. Together with me were the driver, and I don't recall his name, Enes Pojskic, inspector from the security service centre in Zenica, and Ramo Vatres, a criminal investigation inspector from the Territorial Defence headquarters in Vitez. And there is a record of this, which I handed over to the Prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And how long were you detained?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: They kept us for a couple of hours, until Mr. Merdan came to negotiate with Mr. Blaskic. And only after that, we were released.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you then able to conduct an investigation into the killing of these men?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: We had to. There was nobody else to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And to whom or to what type of person did you speak, and what type of enquires were you able to make?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: We were only present there on behalf of the Armija, and we helped the investigation team which had come from the security service centre in Zenica. And I was helping my fellow officer, that is, the criminal investigation technician from Zenica, there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And what was the conclusion of the investigation?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: I don't know what their conclusion was, but we subsequently, through operative work, concluded that the possible perpetrator could be -- just a moment, let me try to remember the name -- a member of the Croatian Defence Council, Dragan Botic, who was with them. I don't mean in their company but in the same coffee pub in which they had been on the way to Kruscica, and he must have come out before them and then ambushed them. But those were only our inferences, which are not founded -- which are not based on any evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, when you come to a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. The next thing is to play a small video clip of the arrest or the part detention of this witness. It will take a couple of minutes. It can be done as conveniently now as after the break, as you choose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: After the break. We'll adjourn now for 20 minutes. Mr. Zlotrg, could you remember, in this adjournment and any other adjournments there are in this case, not to speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over? And that does include members of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the unit could very kindly play the video that covers this incident on the 19th/20th of November --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the audiovisual unit would very kindly play the very short video that covers this incident on the 19th/20th of November, '92. There is no transcript for the television programme that is being played; it's a very short extract, it's a news extract. Rather than burden the translation department last night, which has already got a lot on its plate, I hoped that we could either proceed with no translation or with the interpreters here perhaps reading out the headlines as it comes, but there is very little text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Has it got an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's Z2235,1. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's the wrong video. The other one, please. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: (Voiceover) Muslims and Croats, panic-stricken that they would be killed by the Chetniks. The Serbs attacked their village too, and expelled them. They managed to save a few things, and they are going on an uncertain journey. Two women, exhausted, sitting by the road. They have been travelling for hours. They are fleeing their village that was burned. Their husbands and sons remained at the front line. The Croat Muslim forces are too weak to repel the assailants. The mines bother drivers more than the Serb army, and the UN still hasn't reached Travnik for justified reasons. Now the old city is under constant artillery fire from the Serb side. In Travnik, there are 15.000 refugees, 9.000 of them from Jajce. If the Serbs manage to take Travnik, they are going to establish a corridor direct to Sarajevo, which is 20 kilometres away. A few kilometres east of Travnik, in Vitez, as if they had no other worries, the Muslims and the Croats clashed. The Croats killed two Muslims, mistreated seven Croatian policemen. Croatian policemen took the suspects away.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: This is very difficult to read.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. That's as far as I need go.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Zlotrg, can you tell us, please, we saw a car with people getting out of it: Were you shown there?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness's microphone isn't on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Could you turn the microphone on, please. Press the green ...

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Which one were you? It can always be rerun if necessary, but we can probably do it from memory. Which one were you?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: I was behind the driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At the time that you got out of the car, were you free to move, or were you under some control or restraint?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: We were under the control of the military police of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you were taken from there to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Nice, it was a bit too fast, really, to see anything, as far as I'm concerned. Could we have a fixed frame shown on the screen so that we can see it whilst you provide comments?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I would ask the technicians if they can pick it up at the end of the passage we were looking at, in the garage. (Videotape fixed frame shown)

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Zlotrg, can you tell us, please, what is happening, for example, or what was happening at this time, and which person are you?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: I'm the person wearing a long overcoat, and I'm trying to explain to the military policeman that I had agreed with his superior officer that we could pass unhindered in order to carry out an investigation on the scene in connection with the murder of two TO members. However, he took us to the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who are the other people shown in the picture? We can see a uniformed soldier on the right, you with your back to the camera, in the long overcoat, and then who else?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes. To my left is the inspector, Enes Poljskic, from the security services, and the person between the two of us is a member of the Croatian military police, or it's our driver; I can't really tell. It's not a very good photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How many people took you into custody? One, or more than one?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: There were more of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I hope that meets the problem. I'm sorry not to have dealt with it in that way earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: A transcription issue. During the clip, I heard the translator say there were 15.000 refugees going through the city at this particular period of time, but the transcript doesn't appear to carry that. I would just like to note that for the transcriptionists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We come then to December of 1992, the time when the police station in Stari Vitez had been established or was to be established. I'd like you, please, to help us first of all with notes made and records upon which you may be able to rely. First, from a certain point, were there kept in the police station hand-written notes, by you and by other officers, the originals of which still exist and are with you today?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Those are the documents already produced to the Court as Exhibit 332,1 this morning. They start, as we see, on the 23rd of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Secondly, were you obliged to attend upon a judge on the 3rd of October of 1994, to provide detailed answers in relation to a pending case?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the course of being interviewed following a warning as to your -- an advisement as to tell the truth and a warning of the consequences of giving false testimony, in the course of doing that, were you able to list several events, or many events, between December 1992 and April of 1993?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you able then to rely on the original hand-written notes to which we've just referred, and also on other notes then available to you?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Accordingly, the list of events in the document produced to the judge in October 1994 is longer and more comprehensive than simply the list of events contained in the hand-written notes?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the other hand, the entries in the document of December 1994, even where they cover events also covered in the hand-written notes, are frequently shorter and more succinct?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I would invite the Court to do would be to make an exhibit of the judicial statement and to rely on that as the document setting out events between December 1992 and April 1993, both because it's more comprehensive and because it's for the most part a better summary than the original hand-written notes. I can then deal with them briefly, for the most part, and in detail for some.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is there any objection to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Not that we won't deal with on cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then the previous notes, having been exhibited as 332,1, in order that those lodging documents in a chronological sequence can place them in the right place, these should be given 332,2, and I'll distribute them now. If the witness could please look at the B/C/S version of these, and if the usher could be on hand to display on the ELMO the appropriate English-language versions when we come to them, if the document needs to be detached into two parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Zlotrg, I also want you to have this in mind: If it comes about, as we look through the entries and deal with them swiftly, that any of them have no possible connection, in your judgement, with matters that were ethnically based at the time and were simply common crimes, or may have been, will you be good enough to tell us as much, and we will then strike them from the list, which in the English-language version starts at page 5. Mr. Zlotrg, did you understand my request about deleting items that are in no way ethnically connected? As we go through them, not doing all of them at the moment, but just run through them. Will you tell me, or will you tell the Court, if you think that something is simply a common crime? Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In which case, Your Honour, we can deal with this now, I think, really quite swiftly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There is a point by Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm not sure whether the witness is the person who is supposed to look at the events that are listed here and noted here, whether the witness is the person to draw the right conclusion and to say, "This has nothing to do with an ethnic conflict, this is a mere brawl," or "This has something to do with the ethnic conflicts involved." I think that it is up to the Court to rule on that. I think that we should simply ask the witness whether he knows of these events and whether he wrote this, and then of course we are going to cross-examine him about these events. But we do not expect him to be in a position to draw such conclusions. Thank you. (Trial Chamber deliberates)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've considered this, and we think the right conclusion, balancing the need for the witness to give his evidence, he having knowledge of these events, against the fact that we shall be deciding the case and ultimately having to draw conclusions from the evidence, and those conclusions may include decisions on what are ethnically-based crimes and what aren't, we think the simplest way to deal with it is for the witness to give his evidence, and if he's asked about a matter which he thinks is simply a common crime with no ethnic basis at all, he should say so, and we can then pass on to something else. If the Defence then wish to cross-examine about that particular item, of course it's always open to them to do so. Mr. Nice, I hope we can take this as rapidly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There are some 10 or so pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, but the pages that relate to this period only go from pages 5 to 8, I think, or 9, so that it won't take very long, for the most part. But there are some entries that may have to be dealt with in detail, and we may have to go back to the hand-written notes from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Zlotrg, please, then, is it right that on the 16th of December, the house of Aida Pekmic was shot at, from Gradina?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was that a Muslim person?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 24th of December, fire was opened at the newspaper stand belonging to Hajrudin Karic, a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes, between the headquarters of the Vitez Brigade and the headquarters of Mr. Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 27th of December, the hand grenade thrown at the Kalifornija store, is that a Muslim store?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The 30th of December, an explosive device in the bar and grill of Smajo Duzo. Is he a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The 8th of January, 1993, members of the HVO police, commanded by Vlado Jukic, commander of the police station in Vitez, ordered members of the Bosnia-Herzegovina army military police to leave the joint checkpoint at the railway station?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes, but this is Vladimir Jukic. That is the period when the flag of Bosnia and Herzegovina was taken down and when the flag of Croatia remained.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. The 15th of January, the Big Ben building of Muharem Sarajlic came under fire, and is he a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes, and Big Ben is not a building, it's a restaurant.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. The 19th of January, an armed robbery at the private house of Fajim (sic) Mujkic, property stolen. First of all, is that a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes, and his name is Fehim, F-e-h, et cetera, and on that occasion a large amount of gold was taken away, and a pistol as well; family gold, jewellery.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 19th of January, a rifle grenade fired from the direction given of Toljusic at a catering establishment in Platna Vodica owned by Mesa Hurem. Is that a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes, and it is called Fatina Vodica in the part called Kruscica, and his name is not Mesa, but I don't know his first name. But the last name is Hurem, and he is the owner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 20th and 21st of January, a refugee family from Karaula in Nadioci was harassed by a member of the HVO police?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes, Zdravko Tomic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And do you know the ethnic nature of the refugee family?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 20th of January, Buljubasic was stopped at the railway station in an Opel car, with MUP, and remind the Tribunal, please, what "MUP" stands for, MUP registration plates.

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: "MUP," meaning the Ministry of the Interior. But I do not think they had MUP plates. The plates were simply issued -- civilian plates were issued by the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Plates were taken away, as were the registration plates?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And this was a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes, and they were taken away from him because the plates were not issued by a police station of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The 21st of January, an explosive device thrown at the house of Saban Mahmutovic, chief of the Vitez SJB. "SJB" stands for --

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes, he was acting chief in Stari Vitez, of the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The same day, an explosive device planted on the premises of a Sarajevo bank. It's set out that Darko Kraljevic was in charge of the operation, that Croatian members of the Vitez volunteer fire brigade attempted to enter the premises of the Stari Vitez volunteer fire brigade and seize their vehicles, and you name or somebody has named Marijan Strukar from Stari Vitez and others as playing a key role in this operation. The significance of this, please?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
