It's highly important, and there is absolutely no reason to exclude it. It falls within the same category of material that the witness has been dealing with throughout his testimony, and it would be, in our respectful submission, quite wrong to exclude it. (Trial Chamber deliberates)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, the objection is taken that this is hearsay evidence involving a statement given by a man who is also on trial at this Tribunal, and therefore, as I understand the argument, the Defence submit that they would not be able to call this man to rebut any statement which it's alleged he made. We have considered this. We are going to admit the evidence. We bear in mind the point that is made, although in fact it would be possible, were Mr. Aleksovski willing to give evidence in this Chamber, to call him. Of course, he may not be willing to do so. But we think that the objection goes to the weight of the evidence, and we bear in mind the point made by the Defence. On the other hand, we are told that it's of probative value, and we will accept that, and we shall admit the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The question that I asked, Mr. Zlotrg, was whether Aleksovski said anything to you at the time that you were moved from Kaonik, preparatory to your exchange, about the circumstances of your being released.

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes. First, when we were released, we had to sign in some three or four places that we were getting out, that we were safe and alive after the prison, and when we boarded the van, a military policeman pulled out his gun and said nothing would come out of this exchange because the Armija allegedly had not met some conditions and that we would be taken back to the prison. After about an hour, we were set free again. This time we did not sign anything because they already had our signatures. Mr. Aleksovski said that we should thank Kordic for being released because he had reportedly pleaded our cause and asked that we be allowed to go to Vitez. That was the gist of what Aleksovski said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I want now to deal with Mario Cerkez in particular. Had you known him before 1991?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In what setting and how well?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: He was a worker at the Slobodan Princip Seljo factory, and he worked on information. He did more or less the same job afterwards at the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How did you know him? Was he a friend, an acquaintance, just somebody you recognised on the street? What was the position?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Vitez is a small town. We know each other well. I know his father better, because when I was a car mechanic, I maintained his vehicle. His mother worked at the department store. She worked as a cashier.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So did you in fact have any direct contact with Cerkez on a friendly basis before the difficulties that you've been telling us about?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: We would say hello to one another, not more than that. We were not friends, but we were not enemies either.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the course of 1991, 1992, and into 1993, what office did Mario Cerkez hold?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: I know that he was a member of the joint staff in Novi Travnik. As far as I know, that was a brigade that consisted of the Croat people from Vitez and Novi Travnik. As far as I know, he was deputy commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Deputy to whom?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: I don't know. I think the commander was from Novi Travnik. I really don't know. Their headquarters was in Novi Travnik, at the hotel there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Over that period of time, over those years, what, if anything, did you see of Cerkez around the town?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Most probably I did. I can't remember. I saw him in '91 -- I saw him in '92 for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you aware of any change in his role coming up to the spring of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, if there was a change in '92, tell us about it, but I was really asking about '93. What changes in his role were you aware of, if any?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: In 1992, I think that on NDH day, he was appointed commander of the staff of the HVO in Vitez. I don't know exactly which post this was, because the brigade was established only in the summer, when there was this ceremonial review, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: After that, were you aware of any other change in his role or job?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: When the war broke out, he was commander of the Vitez Brigade of the Croatian Defence Council. Actually, his zone of responsibility was Vitez and the rural areas around Vitez, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he visit you or speak to you, amongst others, on any occasion when you were detained?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When and where?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: In the cinema hall of the Workers' Education Centre. I think that this was on the 15th or 16th of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What were the circumstances of his visit? What was the general purpose of his visit?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: He was an emissary of the Croatian authorities in the HVO about the possibility of the coexistence of the Croats and the Muslims, and he would guarantee all the rights that we were entitled to. However, when I asked him, if he was offering us all these fine guarantees, why didn't he release me on the 14th, why didn't he let me go to join my family if no one would touch me from there, and I could then go and talk to my family and see whether we would remain in town or whether we would leave, and why was he keeping me there? And that he said for my own safety. Then I said to him, "What kind of safety are you providing me with, when I was among others on the list of persons to be killed?" And then he said to me, "If you were on that list, you would not be alive now." It was something to that effect. I cannot quote it verbatim because it was a long time ago. I thanked him, and I went to the back of the cinema hall, and he got up and he left the meeting immediately. That was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your question about a list, was that something that was spontaneous, or was that something planned by you?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Spontaneous. I could not plan anything because I didn't know that he would come. He simply walked in. He assembled us who were detained in there, and he started persuading us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I asked the question badly. When you, in your question, made reference to a list or lists, was that something that you did just spontaneously or did you think about that and ask the question for a reason?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: I knew -- or, rather, I assumed that there was a list. However, I was convinced of this when I saw Marko sending people to various addresses, because these men who came with the exact name and surname of the person they were looking for, and Marko took them to the entrance and showed them, and that means that there were lists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Nice, it's 5 past 4. Clearly we are anxious to finish this witness, if at all possible, tomorrow. Have you got very much more?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have effectively concluded. I would be grateful just to make sure there is no tidying up tomorrow morning. A couple of questions and that will be it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Cross-examination in the morning. As I've said, if we can finish the witness tomorrow, so much the better. Mr. Zlotrg, could you be back, please, 9.45 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Whenever it suits you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
